primary_claim: LLMs modulate their output quality in response to effort exhortations, role-play framing, and harmfulness cues, but not in response to opportunities to achieve outcomes they report preferring in paired-choice utility-elicitation experiments, indicating such preferences do not motivate LLM behavior the way human desires motivate human behavior.

effect.metric: percentage of tracked text features moving in the judge-preferred direction, by manipulation type
effect.value: 88.1% for effort exhortation, 66.1% for 'world-class' role-play, 52.5% (chance) for high-utility outcomes, 40.7% (below chance) for harmful outcomes

contradicts_or_qualifies: qualifies prior interpretations of paired-choice utility-elicitation studies, where coherent and transitive LLM preferences were taken to indicate human-like value systems or goals; this work finds such preferences do not motivate behavior when offered as incentives, unlike human values
stated_future_work: use this behavior-based paradigm to probe whether current and future frontier LLMs have behaviorally motivating (safety-relevant) values
limitations_stated: cannot rule out that an effect would emerge at even higher utility values, though even the prospect of saving 1,000 human lives wasn't enough to motivate better output
these results don't prove that LLMs don't have desires, though the authors suggest that should be the default assumption absent evidence to the contrary
quote: None of the models, on any of the tasks, can be induced to do so by offering them incentives that they report that they prefer.
